content: There is no information provided in the drug label regarding the intravenous (IV) compatibility of medroxyprogesterone acetate when administered orally. Overdosage: Overdosage of combined estrogen and progestin therapy may result in symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, breast tenderness, dizziness, abdominal pain, drowsiness, fatigue, and withdrawal bleeding in women. The treatment for overdose involves discontinuing the conjugated estrogens/medroxyprogesterone acetate (CE/MPA) therapy and providing appropriate symptomatic care. Pharmacology Mechanism of Action: Medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA), when administered either orally or parenterally at the recommended doses to women with sufficient endogenous estrogen, induces the transformation of a proliferative endometrium into a secretory endometrium. The drug exhibits androgenic and anabolic effects but lacks significant estrogenic activity. Parenterally administered MPA suppresses gonadotropin production, thereby inhibiting follicular maturation and ovulation. However, this effect is not observed when the usual recommended oral dosage is administered as a single daily dose. Structure: Medroxyprogesterone acetate tablets USP contain medroxyprogesterone acetate, a derivative of progesterone. It is a white to off-white, odorless crystalline powder that is stable in air and has a melting point between 200°C and 210°C. It is freely soluble in chloroform, soluble in acetone and dioxane, sparingly soluble in alcohol and methanol, slightly soluble in ether, and insoluble in water. The chemical name of medroxyprogesterone acetate is pregn-4-ene-3,20-dione, 17-(acetyloxy)-6-methyl-, (6α)-. Each tablet contains 5 mg, 5 mg, or 10 mg of medroxyprogesterone acetate USP, along with inactive ingredients such as crospovidone, lactose monohydrate, magnesium stearate, methylcellulose, pregelatinized starch, and sodium lauryl sulfate. Pharmacodynamics: Limited information is available in the drug label regarding the pharmacodynamics of oral medroxyprogesterone acetate. Studies have been conducted on the pharmacokinetics of MPA under fasting conditions. In one study, the pharmacokinetics were assessed following a single administration of two 10 mg tablets or a single 5 mg tablet. In another study, steady-state pharmacokinetics were evaluated in 30 postmenopausal women after daily administration of one 10 mg tablet for seven days. In both studies, MPA concentrations in serum were measured using a validated gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) method. The pharmacokinetic parameters of MPA after single and multiple doses were highly variable. 1. Absorption: No specific studies have been conducted to determine the absolute bioavailability of MPA in humans. MPA is rapidly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, with maximum serum concentrations achieved 2 to 4 hours after oral administration. Taking medroxyprogesterone acetate with food increases its bioavailability. A 10 mg dose taken immediately before or after a meal increased the maximum concentration (Cmax) by 50% to 70% and the area under the curve (AUC) by 18% to 33%. The half-life of MPA was not affected by food. 2. Distribution: Approximately 90% of MPA is protein-bound, primarily to albumin. MPA does not bind to sex hormone-binding globulin. 3. Metabolism: After oral administration, MPA undergoes extensive metabolism in the liver, primarily through hydroxylation, followed by conjugation and elimination in the urine.
